summary: This Standards Track document defines a YANG module for a TACACS+ client, extending the system management model from RFC 7317. It lets devices be configured to use TACACS+ servers for centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting, and it can manage TACACS+ over TLS. It obsoletes RFC 9105.

plainLanguage.summary: Many doors need a guard to check who may enter. This is a standard form for telling every door which guard to ask.

subtitle: A YANG module that lets network devices be told which TACACS+ servers to use, now including TACACS+ over TLS.

tldr.problem: Devices that check logins against central TACACS+ servers need a standard, machine-readable way to be configured for it, including the newer TLS-protected form of the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module named ietf-system-tacacs-plus augments the System Management model of RFC 7317 with a list of TACACS+ servers, reusable TLS credentials, source address and VRF settings, and read-only counters.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the earlier RFC 9105 module and adds TLS support. The old shared-secret obfuscation stays only for installed base and is deprecated in favor of TLS.

today: RFC 9950 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026. It obsoletes RFC 9105, so this is the current definition of the module, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a TACACS+ Client Module
sections.content:
The System Management data model in RFC 7317 covers local users and a RADIUS client, but not TACACS+. RFC 9105 filled that gap with a YANG module called ietf-system-tacacs-plus, which augments the System Management model so a device can use TACACS+ servers as an alternative to RADIUS servers.

RFC 9950 is a Standards Track update. It defines a new version of the module that also manages TACACS+ over TLS 1.3 clients, as specified in RFC 9887, and it obsoletes RFC 9105. The module conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices already had a form for telling them which guard to ask. This version of the form adds a way to talk to the guard through a locked, private tunnel.

sections.title: Design of the Data Model
sections.content:
The module is used to configure a TACACS+ client on a device that relies on centralized servers for authentication (checking a username and password), authorization (what commands and privilege levels a user gets) and accounting (recording what the user did).

It augments the /sys:system path with a tacacs-plus container. A device can therefore use local, RADIUS or TACACS+ authentication for users reaching it through a command line or a web interface. The server list holds the TACACS+ servers, and its server-type says whether a server provides authentication, authorization, accounting or any combination. The list is there for redundancy.

Each server can also have a source address, either given directly or taken from an interface, and a VRF instance for servers located in a VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has a list of guards. For each one you write what job it does, such as checking IDs or keeping a visitor log, and which road to use to reach it.

sections.title: TLS Settings and Shared Secrets
sections.content:
For each server, the security choice is either tls or obfuscation. The TLS case follows the requirements of RFC 9887 that the module is designed to cover: TLS 1.3 or later MUST be used, earlier TLS versions MUST NOT be used, cipher suites SHOULD be configurable, raw public keys and pre-shared keys MAY be supported, and the server's domain name MUST be configurable so it can go into the TLS Server Name Indication extension.

The TLS case holds a client-identity (what the client presents), a server-authentication (how the client checks the server) and optional hello-params for TLS versions and cipher suites. Credentials can be written under each server or defined once in client-credentials and server-credentials lists and referenced by name. The module rejects TLS 1.2 as a minimum or maximum version.

The obfuscation case uses a shared-secret string. The module says this is best described as obfuscation, not encryption, because it gives no meaningful integrity, privacy or replay protection. Administrators SHOULD use at least 16 characters and 32 or more is highly recommended. Its use is deprecated in favor of TLS and kept to accommodate installed base.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to talk to a guard. One is a locked private tunnel, which is the good way. The other is a simple scrambled note that anyone clever can read, which is only kept for old doors.

sections.title: Server Parameters and Statistics
sections.content:
The address of a server is an IP address or name, and port is now mandatory. The default port number for legacy TACACS+ is 49, while it is 300 for TACACS+ over TLS, which is why the old default was removed. The domain-name leaf is the name sent in SNI and is distinct from the address used for the connection. sni-enabled can only be set when a domain name is given.

Other leaves include single-connection (Single Connection Mode, off by default) and timeout, the seconds to wait for a server before trying another, with a default of 5. A unique constraint now requires each server to have a distinct address and port pair.

The read-only statistics container counts connection opens, closes, aborts, failures and timeouts, messages sent and received, errors received and sessions. New in this version are discontinuity-time, cert-errors (connection failures due to certificate issues) and rpk-errors (failures related to raw public keys).
sections.plainLanguage: Each guard entry has an address, a door number, and a note saying how long to wait before trying the next guard. There is also a scoreboard that counts how many times each guard was reached or failed to answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed with YANG-based management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have to use a secure transport and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict who may read or write what.

The RFC singles out the server list, because unauthorized access could let an attacker point the device at a compromised TACACS+ server or alter the counters to hide attacks. The shared-secret leaf is protected with default-deny-all, and client-identity and server-authentication with default-deny-write. It names no particularly sensitive readable data nodes or RPC and action operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change the list of guards. If a bad person swapped in a fake guard, they could let themselves into everything.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 9105
sections.content:
Besides TLS support, the changes are: a constraint that servers are unique per address and port, a corrected description of address, a fixed must statement under tacacs-plus, fixes to the example from RFC 9105, a new VRF example, and new examples for TACACS+ over TLS data nodes.

The module revision is dated 2026-03-31. The IANA considerations register the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-system-tacacs-plus and the module name ietf-system-tacacs-plus, with prefix sys-tcs-plus.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a new edition of the form. It adds the tunnel option, fixes a few mistakes and adds more filled-in samples.
